95th Percentile… Is the value below which 95% of the values in the distribution may be found.
Full Width Half Maximum… Is the width of the curve as measured between points on the Y-axis which are at the peak half maximum level.
Note FWHM can be more sensitive to bin count than other statistics. It might not be possible to compute FWHM when the bin count becomes too high and there are not enough bins with values greater than 'Maximum/2'.
Maximum… Is the maximum intensity value within the distribution.
Mean… Is the mean intensity value within the distribution.
Median… Is the median intensity value within the distribution.
Minimum… Is the minimum intensity value within the distribution.
Mode… Is the most commonly occurring value within the distribution.
Otsu Threshold… Is the threshold that separates pixel values into two distinct classes — typically foreground and background — and is determined by minimizing intra-class variance, or equivalently, by maximizing inter-class variance.
Standard Deviation… Is the population standard deviation, which is a measure of the amount of variation or dispersion within a set of values. Shown as the range from the mean value on the histogram.
Note Although both population and sample standard deviations measure variability, there are differences between these two computations. If you are calculating the population standard deviation, then you divide by 'n', which is the number of data values. If you are calculating the sample standard deviation, then you divide by 'n -1', which is one less than the number of data values. This means that the sample standard deviation will have greater variability than that of the population.
Sum… Is the integral of all intensities of all of the pixels.
Dataset
Lets you select the dataset from which values will be extracted.
Show legend
If selected, a legend with the selected measurements will be superimposed on the plotted values.
Copy to Clipboard
Copies the selected statistics to the clipboard, which can be pasted into any word processing or spreadsheet application.
Histogram Tools
The tools at the top of the Histogram dialog let you to pan, zoom, and reset the histogram, as well as save the figure and export data.
Plotting tools
Item
Icon
Description
Pan
Pans or zooms the figure as described below.
Pan… Click with the left mouse button and then drag to pan the figure.
Zoom on the Y axis… Click with the right mouse button and then drag up and down to Zoom in and Zoom out on the Y axis.
Zoom on the X axis… Click with the right mouse button and then drag left and right to Zoom in and Zoom out on the X axis.
Zoom
Zooms to a drawn rectangle, which can be defined by dragging your cursor over the area that you want to zoom.
Reset
Resets the original view of the figure.
Save
Saves the figure as a bitmap image, vector graphic, or in the PDF file format. The figure can also be saved as raw data or PGF code.
Standard image files (*.jpeg, *.jpg, *.png, *.tif, *.tiff extensions)… Saves the histogram or profile as a bitmap image in the screen resolution.
Postscript files (*.eps, *.ps extensions)… Saves the histogram or profile as an encapsulated postscript or postscript file. These types of files have a selectable resolution and provide high-quality graphics for publications.
PGF code for LaTeX (.pgf extension)… Saves the histogram or profile in the Portable Graphics file format. The standard LaTeX picture environment can be used as a front end for PGF merely by using the pgfpict2e package. Requires the XeLaTeX compiler.
Raw RGBA bitmap (*.raw, *.rgba extensions)… Saves the histogram or profile as a raw bitmap image file, in which the file contains only a list of pixel colors and nothing else.
Scalable vector graphics (*.svg, *.svgz extensions)… Saves the histogram or profile in an XML-based vector image format. The SVG specification is an open standard developed by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). SVG images and their behaviors are defined in XML text files.
Portable document format (*.pdf extension)… Saves the histogram or profile in the Adobe PDF file format.
Settings
Opens the Figure options dialog, shown below, in which you can select the plotted ranges, scaling, and labels for the axes.
Edit the Min and Max values for each axis, as required.
Edit the label of each axis, as required.
Choose scaling — Log or Linear — for each axis, as required.
Export to CSV
Exports the plotted values in the comma-separated values (*.csv extension) file format.
How to Analyze a Histogram Extracted From a Shape
Select the required shape in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Click the Histogram button in the Tools box in the bottom section of the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Select the dataset from which the intensity values will be extracted in the Dataset drop-down menu.
The histogram of the selected image data that corresponds to the shape appears.
Do the following, as required.
Select the optimal bin size for the data.
Plot the Y-axis in log scale, if required.
Select the required statistics (see Statistics).
Note You can add a legend to the histogram by checking Show legend.
Adjust the figure with the tools at the top of the dialog (see Histogram Tools).
Note You can also save an image of the histogram or export the plotted data in the CSV file format.

documents.title: Shape Properties and Settings
documents.text:
Shape Properties and Settings
Each shape that is created or imported appears on a separate line in the top section of the Data Properties and Settings panel. You can control the visibility of a shape within a view with the icons available in the top section of the panel, as well as access settings in the lower section to apply effects to selected visuals. A pop-up menu is available that lets you export shapes in the .ORSObject file format, execute a macro, create and extract a structured grid, as well as modify a region of interest (see Shapes Pop-Up Menu).
Shape properties and settings
A. Shape list B. Basic properties panel C. Tools panel D. Shape properties E. Size panel
Shape List
All shapes that can be added to scene views are listed in the top section of the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Click the Shapes icon at the top of the panel to see the available shapes (see Filters for information about filtering the listed items).
Click the Eye icon on the left side of the listed item to show or hide the shape in the current scene. Click the 3D icon on the right side of the listed item to show or hide the shape in the 3D view of the current scene. See Visibility and Color/LUT Controls for more information about changing visibility.
Click the color box to change the color of the lines that define a shape.
Select a shape to see its basic properties and size and to access settings to modify its appearance.
Right-click a shape to access its pop-up menu (see Shapes Pop-Up Menu).
Basic Properties Panel
The information available for the selected shape includes its size, area, and volume. These measurements are calculated as pixels*spacing.
Basic properties
Item
Description
Boxes
Size direction 0, 1, 2… Is the length of each side of the box.
Surface… Is the surface area of the box.
Volume… Is the volume of the box.
Capsules and Cylinders
Height… Is the height of the capsule or cylinder.
Radius… Is the radius of the capsule or cylinder.
Surface… Is the surface area of the capsule or cylinder.
Volume… Is the volume of the capsule or cylinder.
Spheres
Radius… Is the radius of the sphere.
Surface… Is the surface area of the sphere.
Volume… Is the volume of the sphere.
Tools Panel
You can use the Histogram tool that is available in the Tools box to visualize and analyze the distribution of intensity values of image data that intersects with the selected shape (see Plotting Histograms from Shapes).
The Histogram tool is not available for planes.
Shape Properties Panel
The properties available for modifying the appearance of shapes and applying visual effects to selected objects are contained in the Shape properties panel, shown below.
Shape properties panel
If required for a specific workflow, you can set which shape borders and anchors are selectable and can be manipulated. An example of the main code in the Script Runner dialog for setting the state of highlighted table borders is shown below.
Shape properties
Item
Description
Density
Lets you control the spacing within the grid that defines capsules, cylinders, and spheres. Applicable to 3D views only.
Density can be adjusted with the Density slider.
Thickness
Lets you control the thickness of the shape outline in 2D and 3D views and the thickness of the grid that defines capsules, cylinders, and spheres in 3D views.
Thickness can be adjusted with the Thickness slider.
Visual effects
The Visual effects box contains a list of all the available visuals — image data, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, and meshes — to which selected 3D effects can be applied (see Applying Visual Effects to Clips and Shapes).
Edge contrast effect applied outside a box
The Effects properties box displays the properties of the selected effect and includes controls, such as sliders, menus, and color swatches, that you can use to change its properties. You should note that it is possible to apply shape effects to multiple objects and to corresponding data that is either inside or outside of the shape.
Note The visual effects you create with shapes can be included in animated sequences and in screen captures (see Creating Animated Sequences and Exporting Screenshots).
Size Panel
The Size panel, shown below, indicates the parameters associated with the selected shape as well as controls to automatically align the shape to a selected dataset.
Shape properties panel
Size settings and values
Item
Description
Align with dataset
If selected, lets you automatically align the shape along the X, Y, or Z axis of the selected dataset, such as an image, region of interest, or box.
Note Alignments can performed from the center of the shape.
Parameters
Indicates the size of the selected shape, such as its height and radius, as well as positions such as its center point.
Note Positions are shown in the world coordinate system.

documents.title: Shapes Panel
documents.text:
Shapes Panel
In Dragonfly 3D World, shapes such as boxes, spheres, cylinders, and planes can be used for advanced visualization, data clipping, and generating data subsets and masks for targeted analysis. In addition, view splitters let you split the currently selected 3D view into two horizontal windows with an adjustable slider in which you can then apply different 3D visual effects to objects in each half of the view.
Shapes are available on the Shapes panel, shown below.
Shapes panel buttons from left to right: Box, Capsule, Cylinder, Plane, Multiple Planes, Sphere, and Splitter
Shapes can be manipulated, rotated, and resized in 2D or 3D views and can be used in combination to isolate complex volumes.
Boxes… Click the Box icon to create basic box-shaped objects, or cuboids, that have six flat sides. All of their faces are rectangles and all of their angles are right angles.
You can resize and rotate boxes, as well as change their position within a 2D or 3D view with the control points (see Working with Boxes).
Capsules… Click the Capsule icon to create objects consisting of a cylinder with two hemispherical caps on each end. Capsules have the same cross-section from one end to the other.
You can increase or decrease the height and radius of capsules, rotate them, as well as change their position within a 2D or 3D view the control points (see Working with Capsules).
Cylinders… Click the Cylinder icon to create objects with two identical flat ends that are circular and one curved side. Cylinders have the same cross-section from one end to the other.
You can increase or decrease the height and radius of cylinders, rotate them, as well as change their position within a 2D or 3D view the control points (see Working with Cylinders).
Planes… Click the Plane icon to create flat, two-dimensional surfaces that extend to the size of all currently selected visuals. You can rotate planes, as well as translate plane with their handle (see Working with Planes).
Multiple planes… Click the Multiple Planes icon to add three new planes to the Data Properties and Settings panel (see Working with Planes).
Spheres… Click the Sphere icon to create 3D objects shaped like a ball, in which every point on their surface is the same distance from the center.
You can resize the sphere, as well as change its position within a 2D or 3D view (see Working with Spheres).
Splitter… Click the Splitter icon to split the currently selected 3D view into two horizontal windows with an adjustable slider. You can then apply different 3D visual effects to objects in each half of the view (see Working with View Splitters).
Some of the key uses of shapes in Dragonfly include:
Clipping and other 3D effects let you remove data outside or inside a geometry to expose inner structures, such as using a cylinder to isolate a core sample. You can also apply specific 3D effects — such as look-up tables (LUTs), window leveling, or edge contrast — to selected regions of volumetric data, ROIs, or meshes for enhanced visualization of complex structures (see Shape Properties and Settings).
Generated data subsets from specific, geometrically bounded areas can be used for further processing, segmentation or for further analysis.
Shape-based effects, such as a moving clipping plane, can be included in animated sequences and exported in high-resolution images for publications (see Creating Animated Sequences and Exporting Screenshots).
Configured Actions for Shapes
A number of configured actions and keyboard shortcuts are available for editing shapes. The default settings for these actions are listed in the following table.
Default configured actions for shapes
Action
Key
Mouse
Manipulate the clip box
-
Left mouse
Manipulate the capsule
-
Left mouse
Manipulate the cylinder
-
Left mouse
Manipulate the sphere
-
Left mouse
Move the view splitter
-
Left mouse
See Configurable Actions for information about modifying default actions.

documents.title: Shapes Pop-Up Menu
documents.text:
Shapes Pop-Up Menu
A pop-up menu is available that lets you export shapes in the .ORSObject file format, execute macros, create and extract structured grids, as well as modify regions of interest.
Items Available for Single Selections of Most Shapes
The following items are available when you select a single selection of most shapes in the Data Properties and Settings panel. Items uniquely available for different shapes are available in the sections below.
Modify and Transform
The following options are available to modify and transform shapes.
Apply Transformation From… Applies the translate and rotate steps that were previously applied to another shape with the Translate/Rotate tools to the current shape (see Translating and Rotating Objects).
Note The Apply Transformation From function is not available for planes.
Align
Centroid With… Lets you automatically align the centroid of the selected shape with the centroid of another object. Applicable objects include volumetric image data, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, and meshes. These reference objects can be selected in the Choose the Object to Align With dialog.
Note The Align function is not available for planes.
Execute Macro
Provides a shortcut for selecting macros that can be executed for the selected shape.
Extract Object History as Macro
Extracts an object's history as a macro. Extracted macros not only provide an audit trail to help troubleshoot processing issues, but can be edited and replayed to create new objects (see Extracting Object Histories).
Manage User Data
Opens the User Data dialog, in which you can view detailed object descriptions, as well as add fields to further describe the selected shape (see Managing User Data).
Export
As ORSObject… Saves the selected shape in the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format (see Exporting Objects).
Look at Center
Automatically scrolls and zooms so that the selected shape is centered in all views.
Note The Look at Center function is not available for planes.
Extract a One Slice Dataset from Visual Plane
Extracts a 2D image that intersects with the oblique or double-oblique angle of a selected visual plane.
Add to ROI
Labels all voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the current shape and adds them to the selected region of interest.
You can also select New ROI in the Choose an ROI dialog and then choose a name, highlight color, and geometry in the New Region of Interest dialog.
Note In either case, only intersecting voxels will be added to the region of interest.
Note The Add to ROI function is available for all shapes, except planes.
Remove from Structured Grid
Removes all labeled voxels from the region of interest or multi-ROI that intersect with the voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the current shape.
Note The Remove from Structured Grid function is available for all shapes, except planes.
Create a Structured Grid
Lets you create structured grid, which can be an image, region of interest, or multi-ROI, from the volume defined by a box. The inputs can be selected in the appropriate dialog — Create an Image, Create an ROI, or Create a Multi-ROI.
Create an Image dialog
You can select a geometry for all structured grid types, as well as advanced properties that include the object's position in space and its orientation.
For images, you can also select an input data type. Input data types can be the initial value for a uniform image, the common region with the selected reference image, or noise.
Extract Structured Grid
Lets you extract an image from the volume defined by a box, capsule, cylinder, or sphere shape and the intersecting data values of a selected object. You can choose a name and the reference image in the Choose a Name and a Dataset dialog, shown below.
Note The Extract a Structured Grid function is available for all shapes, except planes.
Extract Projection of Structured Grid
Lets you extract 2D projections of images, regions of interest, and multi-ROIs from cylinders and spheres (see Creating Non-Planar Views with Spheres and Cylinders).
Extract 3D Projection of Dataset
Lets you extract 3D projections of images from cylinders and spheres (see Creating Non-Planar Views with Spheres and Cylinders).
Grow to Contain 3D Object
Automatically expands a box to fully enclose the bounding box of a selected 3D object.
You can select the 3D object — such as a mesh, dataset, region of interest, or multi-ROI — that you want to contain or wrap to in the Choose a 3D Object dialog.
Wrap 3D Object
Automatically resizes and reorients a box to tightly wrap the bounding box of a selected 3D object.
You can select the 3D object — such as a mesh, dataset, region of interest, or multi-ROI — that you want to contain or wrap to in the Choose a 3D Object dialog.
Mask Structured Grid
Lets create masks by clearing all labeled voxels from the selected region of interest or multi-ROI that are outside of the shape, or by overwriting image data as the minimum value for its data type. You can choose the required object in the Choose a Structured Grid dialog, shown below.
Note Masks can be used when you need to limit computations to a subset of the data or for training deep models (see Creating Mask ROIs).
Edit Visual Box
Lets you modify the geometry of a Box shape or create a box with a specific granularity. For example, when creating a box for computing vector fields describing anisotropy for a bone analysis.
When you edit a box, you can choose which parameter is locked.
You can also edit the advanced properties of a box, such as its position in space or orientation, in the Advanced Visual Box Properties dialog (see Advanced Dataset Properties). This dialog appears when you click the Advanced Properties button.
Items Available for Multiple Selections
The following items are available whenever you select two or more shapes in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Export
As Multiple ORSObject… Exports the selected items in the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format to a selected folder as multiple files (see Exporting Objects). If the selected items share the same name, their file names will be appended with a sequential number.
As ORSObject… Exports the selected items the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format to a selected folder (see Exporting Objects).
Execute Macro
Provides a shortcut for selecting macros that can be executed for the number of items selected.
Add to ROI*
Labels all voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the current shapes and adds them to a selected region of interest. You should note that only intersecting voxels will be added to the region of interest
Remove from ROI or Multi-ROI*
Removes all labeled voxels from the region of interest or multi-ROI that intersect with the voxels contained in the subvolume defined by the current shapes.
Extract Structured Grid**
Extracts a dataset (structured grid) from the sub volumes defined by the box shapes and the intersecting data values of a selected object.
* Not available if any of the selections are planes.
** Available for boxes only.
Items Available Only for Boxes
The following items are only available for boxes.
Tools
The following menu items let you keep or remove portions of meshes within box shapes.
Keep Inside of Box from Mesh… If selected, portions of the selected mesh outside of the box will be removed.
Cut Inside of Box from Mesh… If selected, portions of the selected mesh inside the box will be removed.
Do the following to modify a mesh:
Create and align a box shape that encloses the area you want to keep or remove.
Right-click the box and choose the required operation in the pop-up menu.
Select the mesh that you want to modify in the Choose the Object to Cut dialog.
Take Box Shape from Feret Of
Reduces a box to the smallest encasing rectangle based on the maximum Feret diameter and minimum orthogonal Feret diameter of the labeled voxels of the selected region of interest or unstructured grid, such as a mesh. You can select the required object in the Choose an Object dialog, as shown below.
Choose an Object dialog
In the illustration below, two box were resized to the Feret and minimal box shapes of selected regions of interest.
Resized boxes
Resized boxes
Take Minimal Box Shape Of
Reduces a box to the minimal encasing rectangle based on the labeled voxels of a selected region of interest or on the bounding box of a mesh.
You can select the required object in the Choose an Object dialog.

documents.title: Shapes
documents.text:
Shapes
Shapes are a series for pre-defined geometrical forms to which 3D effects — such as clipping, window leveling, and edge enhancement — can be applied to selected objects, such as volumetric image data, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, and meshes. A number of operations, such creating masks, extracting sub volumes, as well as generating 2D/3D projections are also available for shapes.

documents.title: Working with Boxes
documents.text:
Working with Boxes
Boxes in Dragonfly 3D World are versatile tools for visualization, data processing, and analysis. They can be used to define, crop, or clip 3D volumes to isolate specific regions of interest, remove unwanted data, or adjust rendering properties. They can also be used for generating data subsets and masks.
The six flat sides of boxes, shown below, can be manipulated independently to create custom clipping planes, while the box itself can be resized, rotated, and translated to perfectly align with specific features in a dataset.
Box shape
Adding and Editing Boxes
Boxes can be used to define, crop, or clip 3D volumes to isolate specific regions of interest, remove unwanted data, or adjust rendering properties in 3D views. They can also be used for generating data subsets and masks (see Box Pop-Up Menu).
How to Add and Edit a Box
Select the object to which you plan to add the box in Data Properties and Settings panel, recommended.
The initial size and orientation of the new box will be modeled on the selected object to provide the best initial fit.
Click the Box button on the Shapes panel.
A new box appears in the Data Properties and Settings panel (see Shape Properties and Settings).
If required, make the box visible by clicking its associated Eye icon in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
The shape appears in the 2D views and 3D view of the selected scene.
Adjust the size and position of the shape, as required.
You can resize and rotate the box, as well as change its position within a 2D or 3D view with the control points indicated and described below.
Lock the shape by checking the Locked option after your adjustments are complete, recommended.
Select the object(s) to which you want to apply 3D effects to in the Visuals box in the Shape properties panel, as shown below.
Select the required 3D effect(s) and adjust their associated properties, as required (see Applying Visual Effects to Clips and Shapes).
Note You can apply the selected effects to the inside or outside of the shape.
Box Pop-Up Menu
A pop-up menu is available for boxes that lets you export shapes, execute macros, modify regions of interest, as well as create, extract, and mask structured grids.
Items Available for Single Box Selections
The following items are available when you select a single box in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Tools
The following menu items let you keep or remove portions of meshes within box shapes.
Keep Inside of Box from Mesh… If selected, portions of the selected mesh outside of the box will be removed.
Cut Inside of Box from Mesh… If selected, portions of the selected mesh inside the box will be removed.
Do the following to modify a mesh:
Create and align a box shape that encloses the area you want to keep or remove.
Right-click the box and choose the required operation in the pop-up menu.
Select the mesh that you want to modify in the Choose the Object to Cut dialog.
Modify and Transform
The following options are available to modify and transform shapes.
Apply Transformation From… Applies the translate and rotate steps that were previously applied to another shape with the Translate/Rotate tools to the current shape (see Translating and Rotating Objects).
Note The Apply Transformation From function is not available for planes.
Align
Centroid With… Lets you automatically align the centroid of the selected shape with the centroid of another object. Applicable objects include volumetric image data, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, and meshes. These reference objects can be selected in the Choose the Object to Align With dialog.
Note The Align function is not available for planes.
Execute Macro
Provides a shortcut for selecting macros that can be executed for the selected shape.
Extract Object History as Macro
Extracts an object's history as a macro. Extracted macros not only provide an audit trail to help troubleshoot processing issues, but can be edited and replayed to create new objects (see Extracting Object Histories).
Manage User Data
Opens the User Data dialog, in which you can view detailed object descriptions, as well as add fields to further describe the selected shape (see Managing User Data).
Export
As ORSObject… Saves the selected shape in the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format (see Exporting Objects).
Look at Center
Automatically aligns and fits all views of the current scene to center the selected box.
Take Box Shape from Feret Of
Reduces a box to the smallest encasing rectangle based on the maximum Feret diameter and minimum orthogonal Feret diameter of the labeled voxels of the selected region of interest or unstructured grid, such as a mesh. You can select the required object in the Choose an Object dialog, as shown below.
Choose an Object dialog
In the illustration below, two boxes were resized to the Feret and minimal box shapes of selected regions of interest.
Resized boxes
Resized boxes
Take Minimal Box Shape Of
Reduces a box to the minimal encasing rectangle based on the labeled voxels of a selected region of interest or on the bounding box of a mesh.
You can select the required object in the Choose an Object dialog, as shown below.
Choose an Object dialog
In the illustration below, two boxes were resized to the Feret and minimal box shapes of selected regions of interest.
Resized boxes
Resized boxes
Add to ROI
Labels all voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the selected shape(s) and adds them to a selected region of interest or to a new ROI.
You can choose a new ROI or existing ROI in the Choose an ROI dialog, as well as choose a name, highlight color, and geometry for new ROIs in the New Region of Interest dialog.
Remove from Structured Grid
Removes all labeled voxels from regions of interest or multi-ROIs that intersect with the voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the current shape(s) or overwrites data values as 0 from image voxels that intersect with the voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the current shape(s).
Create a Structured Grid
Lets you create structured grid, which can be an image, region of interest, or multi-ROI, from the volume defined by a box. The inputs can be selected in the appropriate dialog — Create an Image, Create an ROI, or Create a Multi-ROI.
Create an Image dialog
You can select a geometry for all structured grid types, as well as advanced properties that include the object's position in space and its orientation.
For images, you can also select an input data type. Input data types can be the initial value for a uniform image, the common region with the selected reference image, or noise.
Extract Structured Grid
Lets you extract an image, region of interest, or multi-ROI from the sub volume defined by a shape and the intersecting voxels of the selected object. You can choose a name for the new dataset and the object from which the structured grid will be extracted in the Choose a Name and a Dataset dialog, shown below.
Choose a Name and a Dataset dialog
Note You can also choose an interpolation type — Nearest, Linear, or Cubic — for extracting images.
Grow to Contain 3D Object
Automatically expands a box to fully enclose the bounding box of a selected 3D object.
You can select the 3D object — such as a mesh, dataset, region of interest, or multi-ROI — that you want to contain or wrap to in the Choose a 3D Object dialog.
Wrap 3D Object
Automatically resizes and reorients a box to tightly wrap the bounding box of a selected 3D object.
You can select the 3D object — such as a mesh, dataset, region of interest, or multi-ROI — that you want to contain or wrap to in the Choose a 3D Object dialog.
Mask Structured Grid
Lets create masks by clearing all labeled voxels from the selected region of interest or multi-ROI that are outside of the selected shape, or by overwriting image data as the minimum value for its data type. You can choose the required object in the Choose a Structured Grid dialog, shown below.
Note Masks can be used when you need to limit computations to a subset of the data or for training deep models (see Creating Mask ROIs).
Edit Visual Box
Lets you modify the geometry of a Box shape or create a box with a specific granularity. For example, when creating a box for computing vector fields describing anisotropy for a bone analysis.
When you edit a box, you can choose which parameter is locked.
You can also edit the advanced properties of a box, such as its position in space or orientation, in the Advanced Visual Box Properties dialog (see Advanced Dataset Properties). This dialog appears when you click the Advanced Properties button.
Items Available for Multiple Selections
The following items are available whenever you select two or more box shapes in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Execute Macro
Provides a shortcut for selecting macros that can be executed for the number of items selected.
Export
As Multiple ORSObject… Exports the selected items in the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format to a selected folder as multiple files (see Exporting Objects). If the selected items share the same name, their file names will be appended with a sequential number.
As ORSObject… Exports the selected items the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format to a selected folder (see Exporting Objects).
Add to ROI
Labels all voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the selected shape(s) and adds them to a selected region of interest or to a new ROI.
You can choose a new ROI or existing ROI in the Choose an ROI dialog, as well as choose a name, highlight color, and geometry for new ROIs in the New Region of Interest dialog.
Remove From Structured Grid
Removes all labeled voxels from regions of interest or multi-ROIs that intersect with the voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the current shape(s) or overwrites data values as 0 from image voxels that intersect with the voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the current shape(s).

documents.title: Working with Capsules
documents.text:
Working with Capsules
Capsules in Dragonfly 3D World are versatile tools for visualization, data processing, and analysis. They can be used to define, crop, or clip 3D volumes to isolate specific regions of interest, remove unwanted data, or adjust rendering properties. They can also be used for generating data subsets and masks.
A capsule, shown below, consists of a cylinder with two hemispherical caps on each end. Capsules have the same cross-section from one end to the other.
You can increase or decrease the height and radius of capsules, rotate them, as well as change their position within a 2D or 3D view the control points
Capsule shape
Adding and Editing Capsules
Capsules can be used to define, crop, or clip 3D volumes to isolate specific regions of interest, remove unwanted data, or adjust rendering properties in 3D views. They can also be used for generating data subsets and masks (see Capsule Pop-Up Menu).
How to Add and Edit a Capsule
Select the object to which you plan to add the capsule in Data Properties and Settings panel, recommended.
The initial size and orientation of the new capsule will be modeled on the selected object to provide the best initial fit.
Click the Capsule button on the Shapes panel.
A new capsule appears in the Data Properties and Settings panel (see Shape Properties and Settings).
If required, make the capsule visible by clicking its associated Eye icon in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
The shape appears in the 2D views and 3D view of the selected scene.
Adjust the size and position of the shape, as required.
You can resize and rotate the capsule, as well as change its position within a 2D or 3D view with the control points indicated and described below.
Lock the shape by checking the Locked option after your adjustments are complete, recommended.
Select the object(s) to which you want to apply 3D effects to in the Visuals box in the Shape properties panel, as shown below.
Select the required 3D effect(s) and adjust their associated properties, as required (see Applying Visual Effects to Clips and Shapes).
Note You can apply the selected effects to the inside or outside of the shape.
Capsule Pop-Up Menu
A pop-up menu is available for capsules that lets you export shapes, execute macros, modify regions of interest, as well as create, extract, and mask structured grids.
Items Available for Single Capsule Selections
The following items are available when you select a single capsule in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Modify and Transform
The following options are available to modify and transform shapes.
Apply Transformation From… Applies the translate and rotate steps that were previously applied to another shape with the Translate/Rotate tools to the current shape (see Translating and Rotating Objects).
Note The Apply Transformation From function is not available for planes.
Align
Centroid With… Lets you automatically align the centroid of the selected shape with the centroid of another object. Applicable objects include volumetric image data, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, and meshes. These reference objects can be selected in the Choose the Object to Align With dialog.
Note The Align function is not available for planes.
Execute Macro
Provides a shortcut for selecting macros that can be executed for the selected shape.
Extract Object History as Macro
Extracts an object's history as a macro. Extracted macros not only provide an audit trail to help troubleshoot processing issues, but can be edited and replayed to create new objects (see Extracting Object Histories).
Manage User Data
Opens the User Data dialog, in which you can view detailed object descriptions, as well as add fields to further describe the selected shape (see Managing User Data).
Export
As ORSObject… Saves the selected shape in the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format (see Exporting Objects).
Look at Center
Automatically aligns and fits all views of the current scene to center the selected shape.
Add to ROI

Choose a Name and a Dataset dialog

documents.title: Working with Cylinders
documents.text:
Working with Cylinders
Cylinders in Dragonfly 3D World are versatile tools for visualization, data processing, and analysis. They can be used to define, crop, or clip 3D volumes to isolate specific regions of interest, remove unwanted data, or adjust rendering properties. They can also be used for generating data subsets, masks and 2D/3D projections.
A cylinder, shown below, consists of two identical flat ends that are circular and one curved side. Cylinders have the same cross-section from one end to the other.
You can increase or decrease the height and radius of cylinders, rotate them, as well as change their position within a 2D or 3D view the control points
Cylinder shape
Adding and Editing Cylinders
Cylinders can be used to define, crop, or clip 3D volumes to isolate specific regions of interest, remove unwanted data, or adjust rendering properties in 3D views. They can also be used for generating data subsets and masks (see Cylinder Pop-Up Menu).
How to Add and Edit a Cylinder
Select the object to which you plan to add the cylinder in Data Properties and Settings panel, recommended.
The initial size and orientation of the new cylinder will be modeled on the selected object to provide the best initial fit.
Click the Cylinder button on the Shapes panel.
A new cylinder appears in the Data Properties and Settings panel (see Shape Properties and Settings).
If required, make the cylinder visible by clicking its associated Eye icon in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
The shape appears in the 2D views and 3D view of the selected scene.
Adjust the size and position of the shape, as required.
You can resize and rotate the cylinder, as well as change its position within a 2D or 3D view with the control points indicated and described below.
Lock the shape by checking the Locked option after your adjustments are complete, recommended.
Select the object(s) to which you want to apply 3D effects to in the Visuals box in the Shape properties panel, as shown below.
Select the required 3D effect(s) and adjust their associated properties, as required (see Applying Visual Effects to Clips and Shapes).
Note You can apply the selected effects to the inside or outside of the shape.

Note The Align function is not available for planes.

Provides a shortcut for selecting macros that can be executed for the selected shape.
Extract Object History as Macro
Extracts an object's history as a macro. Extracted macros not only provide an audit trail to help troubleshoot processing issues, but can be edited and replayed to create new objects (see Extracting Object Histories).
Manage User Data
Opens the User Data dialog, in which you can view detailed object descriptions, as well as add fields to further describe the selected shape (see Managing User Data).
Export
As ORSObject… Saves the selected shape in the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format (see Exporting Objects).
Look at Center
Automatically aligns and fits all views of the current scene to center the selected shape.
Add to ROI
Labels all voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the selected shape(s) and adds them to a selected region of interest or to a new ROI.
You can choose a new ROI or existing ROI in the Choose an ROI dialog, as well as choose a name, highlight color, and geometry for new ROIs in the New Region of Interest dialog.

Removes all labeled voxels from regions of interest or multi-ROIs that intersect with the voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the current shape(s) or overwrites data values as 0 from image voxels that intersect with the voxels contained in the sub volume defined by the current shape(s).

Lets you extract 2D projections of images, regions of interest, and multi-ROIs from cylinders and spheres (see Creating Non-Planar Views with Spheres and Cylinders).
Extract 3D Projection of Dataset
Lets you extract 3D projections of images from cylinders and spheres (see Creating Non-Planar Views with Spheres and Cylinders).

Lets you extract an image, region of interest, or multi-ROI from the sub volume defined by a shape and the intersecting voxels of the selected object. You can choose a name for the new dataset and the object from which the structured grid will be extracted in the Choose a Name and a Dataset dialog, shown below.
Choose a Name and a Dataset dialog
Note You can also choose an interpolation type — Nearest, Linear, or Cubic — for extracting images.
Mask Structured Grid
Lets create masks by clearing all labeled voxels from the selected region of interest or multi-ROI that are outside of the selected shape, or by overwriting image data as the minimum value for its data type. You can choose the required object in the Choose a Structured Grid dialog, shown below.
Note Masks can be used when you need to limit computations to a subset of the data or for training deep models (see Creating Mask ROIs).

documents.title: Working with Planes
documents.text:
Working with Planes
You can add planes to a 3D view to clip objects, such as datasets, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, and meshes, along an arbitrary plane or planes. Other visual effects can also be applied to the clipped region, such as look-up table functions, edge contrast, and window leveling. In addition, the explosion options lets you sectionalize 3D renderings to reveal the interior of a sample.
Plane in 3D view
Video Tutorials About Working with Planes
Introduction to Planes Tutorial Video
The following video provides a short tutorial about working with planes.
Introduction to Planes (7:14)
Creating Exploded Views Tutorial Video
The following video tutorial demonstrates how to create exploded views. This video is available at: https://dragonflysocial.comet.tech/c/user-tutorials/how-to-create-explosions-for-advanced-rendering.
How to Create Explosions (2:40)
How to Use Grayscale Mode Tutorial Video
The following video tutorial demonstrates how to use grayscale mode. This video is available at: https://dragonflysocial.comet.tech/c/user-tutorials/how-to-use-the-grayscale-mode-for-visual-planes.
How to Use the Grayscale Mode (1:57)
Shape Properties
As is the case for all other shapes, you can choose the visual effects for the selected plane that you want to apply to selected visuals in the Visual effects box, shown below.
Shape properties
Refer to the topic Applying Visual Effects to Clips and Shapes for information about applying visual effects to image data, regions of interest, multi-ROIs, and unstructured grids.
Plane Settings
The options in the Plane settings box on the Data Properties and Settings panel let you choose an initial orientation for the selected plane or to bind a plane to a 2D view. You can also choose to show corresponding 2D data in the scene’s 3D view, as well as apply an 'explosion' to reveal the interior of a sample.
Plane settings
Plane settings
Item
Description
Orientation
Lets you choose the initial orientation of the selected plane — along the X, Y, or Z axis.
Note As an alternative, you can choose to bind the plane with a view.
Solid
If selected, makes the selected plane semi-solid in order to view the full area covered by the plane, as shown below.
Show data
If selected, data from the corresponding 2D view will be shown on the clipped plane in the 3D view.
Note You must apply clipping in conjunction with 'Show data' (see Shape Properties).
Show grayscale
Applies a grayscale LUT on the clipped plane in the 3D view and lets you adjust the center and width values independently of the window leveling values applied to the dataset.
In some cases, this may provide better results than the 'Show data' method that is also available in Dragonfly. A comparison of the 'Show data' and 'Show grayscale' options is illustrated below, in which a plane with the Show data option applied is shown on the left and with the Show grayscale option on the right.
Note A tutorial video about applying a grayscale LUT to a clipped plane is available in the topic How to Use Grayscale Mode Tutorial Video.
Explosion
Lets you 'explode' 3D renderings to reveal the interior of a sample. You can choose the type of explosion — Translation, Rotation (hinge), or Rotation (screw) — in the drop-down menu, as well as the degree of translation or rotation with the Explosion slider. You can also choose to apply the effect on the left or right side of the plane and to invert rotation explosions.
An exploded 3D rendering is shown in the illustrations below. The dataset exploded by 'Translation' is shown on the left and by 'Rotation (screw)' on the right.
Note A tutorial video about creating explosions is available in the topic Creating Exploded Views Tutorial Video.
Note You can include exploded views in animated sequences and generate high-resolution images with this visual effect.
Bind with view
Lets you link the selected plane to a 2D view. In this case, the controls available in the 2D view, such as the 3D Cursor, can be used to manipulate the plane.
Note The option to bind a plane with a view is dependent on the number of MPR views in the current scene (see Scene Layouts and Views for information about selecting a scene view that includes 2D views).
Adding and Editing Planes
Refer to the following instructions for information about adding and editing planes.
How to Add and Edit a Plane
Make sure that the scene in which you are working includes the 3D view.
You should note that working in a scene with all three MPR views will let you bind a plane to any 2D view.
Do one of the following:
Click the Plane icon on the Shapes panel to add a new plane to the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Click the Multiple Planes icon on the Shapes panel to add up to three new planes to the Data Properties and Settings panel. The number of planes that will be added is equal to the number of 2D views in the current scene.
Select the required plane in the Data Properties and Settings panel and change its visibility in 3D, if required.
The visual plane and its control handle appear in the 3D view.
Choose an initial orientation for the plane or bind the plane with a 2D view, optional.
Adjust the plane as required.
Drag either end of the plane handle to adjust its angle.
Note The object in the illustration above was clipped for clarity. Clipped must be selected as a visual effect to be applied.
You can also adjust the angle of a bound plane by dragging the Angle marker on the 3D cursor in the MPR views of the dataset (see Using the 3D Cursor).
Drag the handle to translate the plane along the selected angle.
You can also translate bound planes by scrolling the associated 2D view or by dragging the 3D cursor in the MPR views of the dataset (see Using the 3D Cursor).
Check the Show data or Show grayscale option for the selected plane, optional (see Shape Properties).
If selected, data from the corresponding 2D view will be shown on the plane in the 3D view.
Reveal the interior of a sample by applying an 'explosion', optional (see Shape Properties).
Select the visuals to which you want to apply the visual effects to.
To apply an effect, check the required object(s) in the Visuals list in the Shape properties panel.
Select the required effect(s) and adjust their associated properties, as required (see Applying Visual Effects to Clips and Shapes).
Note You can apply the selected effects to the outside or inside of the visual plane by checking or unchecking the Outside option.
Lock the plane in the 3D view by checking the Locked option, recommended.
Plane Pop-Up-Menu
A pop-up menu is available that lets you export planes in the .ORSObject file format, execute macros, and extract one-slice images from planes.
Items Available for Single Selections of Planes
The following items are available when you select a single plane in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Modify and Transform
The following options are available to modify and transform shapes.
Apply Transformation From… Applies the translate and rotate steps that were previously applied to another shape with the Translate/Rotate tools to the current shape (see Translating and Rotating Objects).
Note The Apply Transformation From function is not available for planes.
Execute Macro
Provides a shortcut for selecting macros that can be executed for the selected shape.
Extract Object History as Macro
Extracts an object's history as a macro. Extracted macros not only provide an audit trail to help troubleshoot processing issues, but can be edited and replayed to create new objects (see Extracting Object Histories).
Manage User Data
Opens the User Data dialog, in which you can view detailed object descriptions, as well as add fields to further describe the selected shape (see Managing User Data).
Export
As ORSObject… Saves the selected shape in the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format (see Exporting Objects).
Attach Visual Plane To
The selected plane will be resized automatically to the object selected in the Choose the Object to Attach To dialog, shown below.
Extract a One Slice Image from Visual Plane
Extracts a 2D image that intersects with the oblique or double-oblique angle of a selected visual plane and the selected image data. You can select the image to extract the one slice image from in the Choose an Image to Extract From dialog shown below.
Items Available for Multiple Selections
The following items are available whenever you select two or more planes in the Data Properties and Settings panel.
Export
As Multiple ORSObject… Exports the selected items in the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format to a selected folder as multiple files (see Exporting Objects). If the selected items share the same name, their file names will be appended with a sequential number.
As ORSObject… Exports the selected items the Dragonfly Object file (*.ORSObject extension) format to a selected folder (see Exporting Objects).
Execute Macro
Provides a shortcut for selecting macros that can be executed for the number of items selected.

documents.title: Working with View Splitters
documents.text:
Working with View Splitters
View Splitters let you split the currently selected 3D view into two horizontal windows with an adjustable slider. You can then apply different 3D visual effects to objects in each half of the view, such as edge contrast or opacity. You can also clip multiple objects to show an original input on one side and a processed output on the other side.
The video below (https://youtu.be/Ml8ZSytpIbQ?si=T3tFiuAt0wGseT_2) provides a quick introduction to working with View Splitters.
Screenshot of View Splitter video
As shown below on the left, a split 3D view can show the original rendering and with edge contrast applied to the same data. A split view can also contain multiple objects, as shown below on the right. In this case, an original rendering was clipped on one side and a thickness mesh generated from the same data is shown on the other side.
Split 3D view with two rendering effects applied (left) and with multiple objects (on the right)
Click the Splitter button on the Shapes panel to add a 'Splitter' object to the Data Properties and Settings panel and to split the 3D view. You can select the 3D effects(s) that will be applied to the selected object(s) in the left or right window of the split view. The properties available for split views are available in the Shape properties box, as shown below.
Shape properties for splitters
How to Create a Split 3D View
Click the Splitter button on the Shapes panel, as shown below.
A 'Splitter' shape is added to the Data Properties and Settings panel, as shown below, and the 3D view is split into two horizontal windows.
Select the visual(s) with which you are working in the Shape properties box, as shown below.
Note In most cases, you should not select the 3D effect 'Clip' whenever you work with a single visual. This 3D effect is usually used in cases in which you are working with multiple visuals and you need to clip them on alternate sides of the splitter. As shown in the screenshots below, you can clip the selected visual on the right side by leaving the option 'Left side' unchecked and clip the selected visual on the left by checking the option 'Left side'.
Select the required 3D effect(s), as required (see Applying Visual Effects to Clips and Shapes).
Select the 3D effect(s) you chose in the 3D live effects box and then adjust the effect properties, if required (see Applying Visual Effects to Clips and Shapes).
Adjust the position and/or settings of the objects in the 3D view, as required.
Adjust the position of the splitter, as required.
Note You can include sweeps of the split view in animated sequences to show the full transition from one 3D effect to another.
Configured Actions for Splitters
A number of configured actions are available for Splitters. The default settings for these actions are listed in the following table.
Default configured actions for Splitters
Action
Key
Mouse
Move the view splitter
-
Left mouse
See Configurable Actions for information about modifying default actions.

documents.title: Changing the Background and Exporting Screenshots
documents.text:
Changing the Background and Exporting Screenshots
This topic demonstrates how to change the background of the 3D view and how to export screenshots of the 3D view.
This topic continues from Clipping the 3D Rendering (see Clipping the 3D Rendering). You should complete this topic before continuing.
How to Change the Background and Export Screenshots
Select the 3D view if it is not already selected.
Click the Background color button in the Scene's Views Properties panel, as shown below.
The 3D Views Background Color dialog appears, as shown below.
Do the following in the 3D Views Background Color dialog:
Select the Uniform option, as shown below.
Click the Color 1 color swatch, as shown below.
The Select Color dialog appears.
Click the white color swatch in the Select Color dialog, as shown below, and then click the OK button.
Color 1 switches to white.
Click the OK button in the 3D Views Background Color dialog to apply the changes to the background of the 3D view.
Adjust the image in the 3D view, as required.
You can rotate the image, change the applied 3D preset, adjust window leveling, modify the lighting scheme and shadowing, as well as select and adjust the 3D settings (see Optimizing the 3D Rendering).
Do one of the following:
Click the Export Screenshot button on the Scene's Views Properties panel, as shown below.
Right-click inside the 3D view and then choose Export Screenshot of View in the pop-up menu, as shown below.
The Screenshot Size dialog appears.
Enter a new value for the width or height, if required, and then click the OK button.
The Export Screenshot to File dialog appears.
Do the following to save the screenshot:
Select a destination folder and file name for the screenshot.
Select a file format — BMP, JPG, PNG, or TIFF — for the screenshot.
Click the Save button.
Do the following to create multiple screenshots for export:
Select the Camera icon at the top right of the 3D view, as shown below.
Drag the Camera icon to the Multiple Screenshot panel.
A thumbnail of the captured 3D view is added to the Multiple Screenshots panel, as shown below.
Adjust the image in the 3D view. For example, you could rotate the view to show another side of the object.
Drag the Camera icon to the Multiple Screenshot panel.
A new thumbnail is added to the Multiple Screenshots panel.
Add additional screenshots, as required.
Click the Export button, as shown below.
The Export Screenshot to File dialog appears.
Do the following to save the screenshots:
Select a destination folder and file name for the screenshot.
Select a file format — BMP, JPG, PNG, or TIFF — for the screenshot.
Click the Save button.
Click the New Session button on the Task bar, as shown below.
The workspace is cleared and all of the scene views return to their default settings.
Continue to the next topic Creating an Animated Sequence to learn how to create an animated sequence and export it as a video file.

documents.title: Clipping the 3D Rendering
documents.text:
Clipping the 3D Rendering
This topic provides instructions for clipping the 3D rendering and applying 3D effects to the clipped region, such as look-up table functions, edge contrast, opacity, and window leveling. You should note that clipping effects can be included in animated sequences (see Adding Clip Sweeps).
This topic continues from Optimizing the 3D Rendering (see Optimizing the 3D Rendering). You should complete this topic before continuing.
How to Clip the 3D Rendering
Click the Clip button in the Clip box, as shown below. The Clip box is available on the Properties tab on the right sidebar.
A clip box appears in the 3D view.
Note Refer to the topic Clip Tool for detailed information about using the Clip tool.
Check the options Tone mapping and Filtered gradient in the 3D settings box, as shown below.
These settings will help optimize the visualization of the clipped region (see 3D Settings).
Do the following to clip the data:
Hover over a face of the clip box to activate it, as shown below.
Drag to clip the data, as shown below.
Click the Clip button again to remove the clip box from the view.
Note The clipping effect will be retained when the clip box is removed from the view.
Make any required adjustments to window leveling and lighting to optimize the clipped rendering. You can also zoom and pan the image to center it in the view.
Expand the Visual effects section in the Clip box, as shown below.
Note Refer to the topic Applying Visual Effects to Clips and Shapes for information about working with the available visual effects for clips.
Uncheck Clip and then check Edge Contrast, as shown below.
Select Edge Contrast in the 3D live effects list and then adjust the effect with the slider, as shown below.
The selected magnitude of the effect is applied to the clipped region, as shown below.
Click the Reset button, as shown below, to reset the clip box.
The Clip box is reset.
Continue to the topic Changing the Background and Exporting Screenshots to learn how to change the background colors and export screenshots of the 3D view.

documents.title: Creating an Animated Sequence
documents.text:
Creating an Animated Sequence
This topic describes how to create an animated sequence in the Movie Maker and export it as a video file. You create animated sequences by adding key frames to the timeline that define camera effects such as zooms, pans, and rotations, as well as other property transitions, such as window leveling, clipping, and opacity (see Movie Maker). The timing of transitions between key frames can be adjusted on the timeline and the gaps between key frames, or control points, will be interpolated to result in a smooth animation.
You created a new session at the end of the last topic. You will need to reload the data to follow this last topic in the series.
How to Create an Animated Sequence
Choose File > Import Image Files on the menu bar.
The Import Image dialog appears.
Click the Recent Files button and then choose the walnut image stack files in the drop-down menu, as shown below.
All of the files in the stack are added to the Import Image dialog.
Click Next to continue.
The next screen appears.
Edit the image name so that it is simply 'walnut' instead of 'walnut001'.
Click Finish.
The imported image group appears in the default scene view layout.
Double-click the 3D view. This will maximize the 3D view in the workspace, as shown below.
Optimize the 3D rendering, as described in the topic Optimizing the 3D Rendering, and remove the legend from the view.
Right-click inside the 3D view and then choose Show Movie Maker in the pop-up menu, as shown below.
The Movie Maker panel appears in the workspace, as shown below.
Rotate the image in the 3D view and then click the Add Key button on the Movie Maker panel, as shown below.
A new key frame is added to the Movie Maker timeline, as shown below.
Click the Rotate button, as shown below.
The Rotation Options dialog appears.
Select the Rotate Around Y Axis rotation option, as shown below.
Note Refer to the topic Adding Rotations for additional information about adding rotations to an animated sequence.
Click the OK button.
A new key frame is added to the Movie Maker time line. The small indicators that appear at the bottom right of the linked key frames, circled below, indicates that they are linked by a rotation.
Click the Clip Sweep button and then choose Clip sweep along X- in the drop-down menu, as shown below.
A clip sweep is added to the timeline, as shown below.
Click the Start button, as shown below, to move the Seek bar to the beginning of the animated sequence.
Click the Play button, as shown below, to preview the animated sequence.
Note Refer to the topic Editing Animated Sequences for information about editing an animated sequence, such as adjusting timing and modifying key frames.
Click the Export Animation button to export the animated sequence.
The Export Animation dialog appears.
Click the Save as Video File button in the dialog.
Note Refer to the Help topic Exporting Animated Sequences for information about the recording options. In this tutorial, you will be asked to save the file with the default settings.
Do the following to save the animated sequence:
Select a destination folder and file name in the Export As Video File dialog.
Click the Save button.
Wait for the animated sequence to be exported and then close the Export Animation dialog.
Right-click inside the 3D view and then choose Close Movie Maker in the pop-up menu, as shown below.
View the saved video file in an external application, such as Windows' Media Player.

documents.title: Importing Generic Raw Files
documents.text:
Importing Generic Raw Files
This tutorial will guide you through importing a generic raw file. To import a generic RAW file, you must provide the Image Loader with information about the data contained in the file, such as the image size and data type. These settings are outlined in the following table.
Image settings for raw data
Item
Description
Size (in pixels)
Provides the size of the data in the X, Y, and Z axes.
Data type
Indicates the numeric data type — unsigned/signed char, unsigned/signed short, unsigned/signed int, float — in which the raw data was saved.
Reverse byte ordering
You can reverse the byte ordering by checking this box. Applicable only if Unsigned short, Unsigned int, or Float is selected as the data type.
Signed data
If you selected an unsigned data type, you can have the data interpreted as being signed by checking this box.
Offset into file
You can insert an offset to where the raw data really starts by entering a value in this edit box. You should note that offsets typically occur in PIC files, in which the raw data co-exists with header data. For most other image files, no offset ('0') will produce the best results.
How to Import a Generic Raw File
Download and extract the raw data featured in this tutorial. The data is available in a Zip file at: https://theobjects.com/dl/walnut-raw.zip.
Choose File > Import Image Files on the menu bar.
The Import Image dialog appears.
Click the Add button, as shown below.
Navigate to the folder that contains the downloaded raw data.
Select the 'walnut.raw' file in the Add File(s) dialog.
Click the Next button to continue.
The next screen appears, as shown below.
Enter the following settings in the Size (in pixels) box:
X: 400
Y: 296
Z: 352
Choose Unsigned short (16 bits) in the Data type box.
The preview of the raw data is updated, as shown below.
Note Refer to the topic Settings for Importing RAW Files for more information about the additional settings available for importing raw files.
Click the Next button to continue.
The next screen appears, as shown below.
Enter values of 0.20 mm for the X, Y, and Z axes in the Image spacing box, as shown below.
Note Refer to the topic Image Settings for information about the additional settings available here.
Click the Finish button to import the selected data.
When processing is complete, the imported data will appear in the default workspace view layout. Refer to the topics in the section Visualizing Images for information about the tools available for visualizing and inspecting your data.
Note You can also follow the Getting Started Tutorial with the loaded raw data. This detailed tutorial provides topics about visualizing data, optimizing 3D renderings, clipping, exporting screenshots, and creating animated sequences.

documents.path: Tutorials/Importing Raw Data From Comet Yxlon CT Systems.htm
documents.title: Importing Raw Data From Comet Yxlon CT Systems
documents.text:
Importing Raw Data From Comet Yxlon CT Systems
This tutorial will guide you through importing raw data saved on a Comet Yxlon CT system. The simplest way to load reconstructed projection data is to import the text file that references the raw data. This file, which is usually saved as '.cvolume.raw.volumeinfo' in the output ReconData directory, provides the settings needed to open the referenced raw data correctly.
How to Import Raw Data From a Comet Yxlon CT System
Choose File > Import Image Files on the menu bar.
The Import Image dialog appears.
Click the Add button, as shown below.
Navigate to the folder that contains the required raw data. For example, ReconData > CERA_YYYY.MM.DD-HH.MM.SS.
Select the required '.cvolume.raw.volumeinfo' file in the Add File(s) dialog, as shown below.
Click the See Preview button to preview the selected file, optional.
Note information about the composition of the associated raw data — such as the size of each axis in pixels and data type — is extracted and displayed for reference purposes. In addition, a Z-Slice slider, circled below, is available for scrolling through the data.
Click the Next button to continue.
The next screen appears, as shown below.
Note Refer to the topic Image Settings for information about the settings available on this screen.
Do the following, optional.
Enter a name for the imported data in the Image group box.
This is the name that will appear in the Data Properties and Settings panel to identify the imported data.
Enter an image sampling rate for the X, Y, Z axes in the Image sampling edit boxes, if required (see
Image sampling).
Note If the total size of the dataset exceeds your system's capabilities, you will have to sample the data. Information about the dataset size and dimensions is available in the Information box.
Enter any required Offset and Slope values in their respective boxes (see
Physical conversion).
Note In most cases, the optimal Offset and Slope values are 0 and 1, respectively.
Click the Crop Image button in the Transform box, if you need to crop your data (see Cropping Image Data).
Click the Finish button to import the selected data.
When processing is complete, the imported data will appear in the workspace view(s) by default. Refer to Visualizing Images for information about the tools available for visualizing and inspecting your data.
Note You can also follow the Getting Started Tutorial with the loaded raw data. This detailed tutorial provides topics about visualizing data, optimizing 3D renderings, clipping, exporting screenshots, and creating animated sequences.

documents.title: Importing the Image Stack
documents.text:
Importing the Image Stack
This topic provides step-by-step instructions for importing the stack of 2D image files that will be used in the following topics of this tutorial.
How to Import the Image Stack
Download the image data that will be featured in this tutorial. The data is available in a Zip file at: https://theobjects.com/dl/walnut-stack-tiff.zip.
Unzip the file that you downloaded.
Launch Dragonfly 3D World.
Choose File > Import Image Files on the menu bar.
The Import Image dialog appears.
Click the Add button, as shown below.
Note Refer to the topic Import Image for more information about the options available on the first screen of the Import Image dialog.
Navigate to and select the folder in which you saved the walnut image stack.
Select all of the files in folder by pressing Ctrl-A and then click the Open button, as shown below.
All of the TIFF image files in the folder are added to the Import Image dialog.
Click Next to continue.
The next screen appears.
Edit the image name so that it is simply 'walnut' instead of 'walnut001', as shown below.
Note Refer to the Help topic Image Settings for information about selecting the settings for image sampling, image spacing, offset and slope, axis transforms, as well as cropping an image. You can also import another image by checking the Import another image option.
Click Finish.
The imported image group appears in the default scene view layout and is listed in the Data Properties and Settings panel on the right sidebar, as shown below.
You can change the view layout by selecting another option in the Layout panel, shown below.
Note Refer to the topic Scene Layouts and Views for more information about selecting layouts and the setting preferences for the default view layout.
Continue to the topic Visualizing the Data in 2D to learn how to visualize and manipulate the data in the 2D views.

documents.title: Optimizing the 3D Rendering
documents.text:
Optimizing the 3D Rendering
This topic describes how to optimize the 3D rendering of the image stack and how to apply clipping and edge contrast to reveal the inside of the rendering.
This topic continues from Visualizing the Data in 2D (see Visualizing the Data in 2D). You should complete this topic before continuing.
How to Optimize the 3D Rendering
Click the button shown below to split the workspace into four views, with the 3D view as the largest at the top of the workspace.
The views in the workspace are updated.
Click anywhere inside the 3D view to make it active.
Drag the Window Leveling text annotation to remove any remaining voxels of the background, as shown below.
Note Refer to the topics in Window Leveling for information about adjusting window leveling and using the advanced controls on the Window Leveling panel.
Choose Grayscale (solid) 2 in the Presets dropdown menu in the 3D presets box, as shown below. The 3D presets box is available on the Properties tab on the right sidebar.
The settings of the preset are applied to the image in the 3D view.
The Grayscale (solid) 2 preset includes lighting and shadows, as shown on the Scene's Views Properties panel on the Main tab, and settings for Solidity, Diffuse, Specular, and Shininess in the 3D settings box on the Properties tab.
Note The options in the Lighting box let you change the direction and intensity of the light illuminating objects in a 3D view, as well as to add multiple lights to help achieve a higher degree of photo realism and better shadow detail (see Lighting Properties). You should note that many of the lighting options produce the best results when used in combination with material properties such as shininess, specular, and diffuse (see 3D Settings).
Do the following to improve the applied lighting and shadows:
Click and drag anywhere on the Light widget to change the direction of illumination of the selected light.
Adjust the shadow strength and opacity, as shown below.
Add an additional light, as shown below.
Select the additional light and adjust its position, intensity, and shadow strength and opacity.
Do the following to adjust the 3D settings:
Use the sliders in the 3D settings box to adjust the material properties of Solidity, Diffuse, Specular, and Shininess, as shown below.
Check the Edge contrast option and then adjust the level with the slider, as shown below.
The rendering will become less opaque as you make your adjustments, as shown below.
Uncheck the Edge contrast 3D setting.
Do the following to adjust the view by zooming in and out:
Hold down the middle mouse button (scroll wheel).
Drag up or down to adjust the applied zoom factor.
Do the following to rotate the view:
Hold down the left mouse button.
Drag to rotate the view, as shown below.
Do the following to pan (move) the view:
Hold down the left and right mouse buttons.
Drag to position the walnut in the center of the view.
Note If you prefer to not work with shortcuts, you can also select the Pan and Zoom buttons on the Manipulate panel to make your adjustments. After using one of these tools, you can go back to the default Track state by pressing Esc on your keyboard or by clicking the Track button.
Uncheck the Show legends option in the Scene's Views Properties panel, circled below, to remove the legend from the views.
Continue to topic Clipping the 3D Rendering to learn how to reveal the inside of a 3D rendering with the Clip tool.
